\chapter{Comer Es Bueno --- The Infinitive as Subject}
\label{ch:comer-es-bueno}
\hlchaptermodality{264}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name an activity and say something about it.}

I can name an activity and say something about it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comer es bueno]{comer es bueno — the infinitive as the subject}

\label{lesson:ES-C67-comer-es-bueno}



\begin{quote}
\emph{El libro es grande.} A noun, then \emph{es}, then what it is.

Now put an \textbf{action} in the noun's place.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the infinitive stands there}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Comer}} \emph{es bueno.} — Eating is good. \emph{\textbf{Hablar}} \emph{español es bueno.} — Speaking Spanish is good.
\end{quote}

The infinitive — the plain dictionary form — simply occupies the subject slot, and the sentence carries on as normal. Nothing is added and nothing changes shape.

Note the verb after it: \emph{\textbf{es}}, singular. An action counts as one thing, however many words are wrapped around it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Here is the trap, and it is entirely an English one.

English uses \emph{-ing} for this — \emph{eating is good} — and you have an \emph{-ing} form now. So it is tempting to reach for \emph{\textbf{comiendo}}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Comiendo es bueno.} — \textbf{wrong.}
\end{quote}

The gerund never does this job in Spanish. It is for an action \textbf{underway}, leaning on \emph{estar}; it is not a name for the activity. The infinitive is the name.

So the two languages divide the work differently, and Spanish's division is the simpler one: English argues about \emph{to eat} against \emph{eating}, and Spanish uses one form for both.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Comer es bueno}
  \item \emph{Hablar español es bueno}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form names an activity — the infinitive or the gerund? (The \textbf{infinitive}.)

And what is the gerund for? (An action \textbf{underway}, with \emph{estar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
